title: Find a Value in a Sorted List
statement:
You get a list nums of distinct integers sorted from smallest to largest, and a number target.

Return the index where target sits in nums, or -1 if it is not there.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time. Walking the list from the start is not enough.

examples.why: The middle is 0, which is too small, so the whole left half is dropped. Two more halvings land on 11.
3 would sit between 0 and 5. The search ends when the range is empty, without ever seeing a 3.
The answer is the last index. A loop that stops while one candidate is still left (lo < hi with an inclusive hi) never checks it.

constraints: All values in nums are distinct and sorted ascending
hints: Compare target with the middle value. Which half can you throw away, whatever the answer turns out to be?
Keep two indexes lo and hi that bound the part of the list where target could still be. Decide exactly what they mean before writing the loop.
With an inclusive range [lo, hi], loop while lo <= hi. If nums[mid] is too small, move lo to mid + 1; if too big, move hi to mid − 1. When lo passes hi, the range is empty.

explain.intuition:
Sorting lets one comparison speak for many values. If the middle value is smaller than target, every value to its left is smaller too, so half the list is gone after one look. Halving 100 000 items reaches 1 after about 17 steps.

The hard part is not the idea but the edges. Write down what lo and hi mean and keep that promise on every line. The usual choice is inclusive: target, if present, is somewhere in nums[lo..hi]. Then the range is empty only when lo > hi, so the loop runs while (lo <= hi). And since mid itself has been checked, the new bound is mid + 1 or mid − 1, never mid. Every off-by-one bug in binary search comes from mixing two different meanings of hi.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = n − 1. Promise: if target exists, its index is in [lo, hi].
While lo <= hi (the range still holds at least one index), take mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2).
If nums[mid] < target, everything up to mid is too small: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise hi = mid − 1.
When the loop ends the range is empty, so return -1.
pitfalls: Writing while (lo < hi) with an inclusive hi. The loop exits with one unchecked index left, and [2, 6, 9] with target 9 returns -1.

Setting hi = mid in the inclusive version. When lo === hi and the value is too big, mid stays the same and the loop never ends. In the half-open version [lo, hi) the rule flips: hi = mid is right and the loop is while (lo < hi).

Computing mid as (lo + hi) >> 1 when lo + hi can pass 2³¹ − 1 (about 2.1·10⁹). JavaScript bit operators work on 32-bit integers, so the sum wraps to a negative number. For array indexes it is safe; for searching a value range use lo + Math.floor((hi − lo) / 2).

solutions.title: Walk the list
solutions.idea: Check every index from the left. Correct, but it ignores the sorting and takes O(n).

solutions.title: Binary search, inclusive range
solutions.idea: lo and hi are both possible answers. Loop while the range is non-empty (lo <= hi) and move past mid on every step.

solutions.title: Lower bound, half-open range
solutions.idea: Find the first index whose value is >= target, keeping the range [lo, hi) with hi excluded. Then check whether that index holds target. The same loop answers 'where would it be inserted'.

followups: The values may repeat. Return the first and the last index of target. How do the two searches differ?
The list is too large to know its length (an infinite stream you can index). How do you find a range to search in?
